author: pcaversaccio
content: <@425274498732916736> creating a thread here - against the finalised (and frozen) upgrade spec. the point would be to formally establish that the client impl of the hard fork correctly implements the specified state transition and consensus rules, rather than merely relying on tests & cross-client agreement. ofc this also raises the harder q of how we gain confidence that the spec itself is correct, but i see impl-to-spec verification as a meaningful first step.

author: pcaversaccio
content: maybe we could consider Geth as the ground truth spec?

author: potuz
content: FWIW I did not mean to sound like talking "down" at you <@840207942581747712> but rather I think that formal verification methods are better used "one step above". I think it'd be great to have a formally verified forkchoice specification.. be absolutely certain that 1/3 of the stake is slashable if two contending branches finalize, be certain that justification is strictly increasing, etc.. I think it becomes much harder to have these methods being useful at the client level. There's a push to have the pure STF to be formally verified, mostly in the lean world where the STF itself will be a black box that even node implementers would not be able to understand nor diagnose. But as <@543900561460822016> correctly points out, a node is much more than the core STF, and our bugs are typically outside of there

author: sky.cactus
content: There should be no single "ground truth".  If spec, tests, or clients disagree with any of the others, then intelligent reasoning beings who know the *intent* should stop and analyze the situation and decide which is the correct one.  We should be careful to *never* blindly follow any one source (even a specification).

author: pcaversaccio
content: ok let me ask in another way (most of my "practical" experience/knowledge is based on formally verifying the vyper compiler): where could we best leverage formal verification methods for hard forks currently?

author: pcaversaccio
content: for example yesterday i talked to the Qubes maintainers as i try to push fv methods for OSes as well and we agreed that most hardening via fv makes sense in parts that are an attack surface, not just have high privileges. that means parts that are crossing VM boundaries, various APIs etc. that may make sense for example for qrexec, qubesdb, and possibly few more. could we also use such an incremental approach?
